topic: Headline vs core inflation: the index basket, why food and fuel are taken out for core, what each measures, why 'headline' is so called, and India's headline index

food and fuel: volatile prices, transitory causes
core inflation = index without food and fuel
concepts.prereq_recalled: food and fuel distort the true picture

concepts.name: headline inflation = index with food and fuel
headline vs core: total inflation vs long-run trend
why 'headline': the rate reported in media
India's headline index: WPI till 2014, CPI-C from Feb 2015

book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook usually defines both terms in one sentence each and then explains why food and fuel are excluded. Here the reason comes first: the basket is shown, two parts are marked as jumpy, economists' worry ('true picture nahi milega') is voiced, and only then is the trimmed basket named core, with headline defined as 'the one that still has them'. The name's origin (newspapers) is kept as a closing 'interesting fact', and India's switch from WPI to CPI-C comes last as data.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Start from one whole (the index basket), find the part that causes trouble, remove it, and name the whole and the remainder as the two terms.

narration.density: About 13 terms (inflation index, component, commodity basket, food, fuel, transitory, volatile, true picture, core inflation, headline inflation, total inflation, long-run trend, WPI, CPI-Combined) in about 145 s of teaching, about 5 per minute. The terms are light and the bar carries the main pair, so the pace suits class 9 up; for younger learners it lacks a single number example (headline 7% vs core 4%).

talmel_summary: At the core of the video picture and voice land together: FOOD and FUEL are written on their words, the red crosses fall on 'food aur fuel', the bar shrinks on 'bina food aur fuel', and the CORE and HEADLINE chips land within 0.6 s of their names, so the definition is seen as subtraction. Elsewhere the picture runs ahead or stands still: the bar, its copy and the frames are built in a 12 s stretch with no recognised speech, the 'volatile & transitory' label comes 12-35 s before those words, the definition text appears before the spoken answer, and two long still stretches (31-65 s and 90-113 s) carry the causes and the key comparison by voice alone.

voice.notes: About 148 words per minute over the whole video (including a 12 s silence or lost stretch at 12.6-24.4 s); calm, plain, conversational Hinglish with English terms (component, transitory, volatile, long run trend). Stress falls on 'true picture' and 'long run trend'. The only numbers are years (2014, February 2015), read in English. The closing 'interesting fact' is said with a lift, as a small reward at the end.

game_ideas.player_does: Runs a month-by-month price monitor with a basket bar of goods (cereals, vegetables, petrol, cooking gas, clothes, rent, medicines). Shock cards arrive (weak monsoon, crude oil spike, good harvest); the player drags items out of the basket to build a 'core' bar.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each month the item blocks jump or stay; two lines run on a chart: headline (whole basket) and core (the player's trimmed basket).
game_ideas.win: Core line stays smooth while headline jumps with the shocks, because exactly the volatile items (food, fuel) were removed.
game_ideas.lose: Removing a steady item (rent, clothes) makes core lose part of the real trend; keeping vegetables or petrol in core makes core jump on every monsoon or oil shock, and the 'true picture' badge cracks.
game_ideas.concept: core inflation = index without food and fuel

game_ideas.player_does: Acts as a newspaper editor: given a month's headline and core figures and a news ticker (vegetable prices up 30%), chooses which number goes on the front page and writes the cause under it.
game_ideas.process_happens: The front page prints the chosen figure; a reader asks 'is inflation really rising long-term?' and the core line answers.
game_ideas.win: Headline figure on the front page, food spike named as the cause, core named as the long-run trend.
game_ideas.lose: Printing core as 'headline' or calling a one-month food spike a long-run trend shows the trend line flat and the reader misled.
game_ideas.concept: headline vs core: total inflation vs long-run trend

game_ideas.player_does: Places index chips (WPI, CPI-Combined) on India's timeline as the headline measure.
game_ideas.process_happens: The newspaper icon above the timeline changes which index it quotes as the chip is placed.
game_ideas.win: WPI before the switch, CPI-C after it, with the switch dated (date to be checked: April 2014 adoption, February 2015 agreement).
game_ideas.lose: A wrong order makes the newspaper quote a wholesale index for a consumer price story, and the mismatch is pointed out.
game_ideas.concept: India's headline index: WPI till 2014, CPI-C from Feb 2015

checks_learned: A still canvas longer than about 20 s while the narration gives new causes or the key comparison must be flagged; each spoken cause (transitory factor, rain) needs its own picture.
A label must not appear long before its words: 'volatile & transitory' came 12-35 s early; keep a label within about 2 s of the term.
When the narrator asks the viewer a question, the answer text must wait for the spoken answer (here it appeared 2.7 s before).
The same item must keep one name in speech and on screen (spoken 'energy' vs on-screen 'fuel').
A comparison of two measures should carry one number example (headline x% vs core y% in the same month) so the difference is seen, not only stated.
Branded newspaper pages and real mastheads must be redrawn as generic newspapers.
Dates of policy switches written on screen (CPI-C 'since Feb 2015') must be checked against a source before reuse.
A transcript stretch of more than 5 s with no words (12.6-24.4 s, 41.3-46.6 s) flags lost or missing narration in BIE's own audio checks.

teaching_best.why: The definition is taught as an action: food and fuel are crossed out of the basket and the shorter bar is named core, so 'core = headline minus volatile items' is seen.
The reason comes before the term: economists' worry that volatile items hide the true picture is voiced first, and core arrives as the fix.
Headline is defined against core in one line ('the one that still includes food and fuel'), tying the two terms to the same bar.
A small 'do you know why' question about the name, answered with newspapers, gives an easy memory hook.

teaching_weak.why: Causes of volatility (transitory factors, the season's rain) and the economists' argument are spoken for about 34 s over a still picture.
No number example anywhere: 'total inflation vs long-run trend' is said, never shown with figures or a chart.
The definition text gives away the answer before the narrator answers his own question.
The WPI-to-CPI-C switch is given as 'till 2014 / from February 2015' without explaining the gap; usually dated to RBI's April 2014 adoption with the February 2015 agreement formalising it (verify).
No recap and no exam link; the video ends on a plug.
